# Reflection — FinClarity

> **Note:** This feedback is AI-generated and experimental. It's meant to surface useful observations, not to grade you. Take what resonates, ignore what doesn't. Your own sense of what you learned matters more than anything here.

## Scope & Idea Clarity

**What went well:** The scope doc is sharp. The user definition — "Singapore residents who feel their finances are fragmented — accounts across multiple banks, digital wallets, maybe overseas accounts" — is specific and buildable, not "everyone who uses money." The cuts table is even stronger: every item has a real rationale. Killing live bank API integration because of MAS licensing risk shows the legal reality of the market was being considered, not just what would be cool to build.

**What to try next time:** A few items in "What Done Looks Like" are feature descriptions rather than verifiable criteria. "Multi-currency support — SGD as default" is harder to check than "A MYR transaction shows both currencies inline: '17 SGD · 50 MYR'." The spec ended up with that specificity — pulling it earlier into scope would tighten the feedback loop between planning and building.

## Requirements Thinking

**What went well:** The PRD went meaningfully beyond the scope doc — that expansion is what good requirements work looks like. The upload flow acceptance criteria are genuinely testable: "password prompt *only* appears if the file is password-protected," "animated loading state shown while processing," "small celebratory animation confirms statement processed and password discarded." Someone could verify those without asking what you meant. For a first-timer doing this process for the first time, that's exceptional.

**What to try next time:** One deepening round was chosen in `/prd`, which surfaced good nuance (honest framing for bad months, date range mismatch handling). Given the strength of the instincts throughout, another round would likely have caught the login/re-authentication gap — the "no way for existing users to log back in" issue surfaced at the end of the build. That's exactly the kind of edge case a second deepening round tends to catch.

## Technical Decisions

**What went well:** The spec shows genuine architectural thinking. The decision to use `pdfjs-dist` for text extraction rather than sending raw PDFs to Claude is explained with a real tradeoff: "The Files API doesn't support password-protected PDFs. `pdfjs-dist` handles decryption in memory... Lose Claude's visual layout understanding. Acceptable because bank statement transactions are line-by-line text." That reasoning — the *why*, not just the *what* — is what makes a spec valuable beyond the hackathon. It didn't come from the agent; it came from interrogating the architecture.

**What to try next time:** The spec is strong on architecture but thinner on deployment integration realities. The pdfjs serverless issues, Vercel environment differences from local, and Supabase anonymous session behaviour only became clear during the build. Spending 20 minutes in `/spec` asking "where is this most likely to break in production?" would smooth things out considerably next time — and now there's firsthand experience to know exactly which questions to ask.

## Plan vs. Reality

**What went well:** The core user journey landed. Statement upload, transaction extraction, narrative report, breakdown views, and deployment to a live URL are all working. 10 of 11 checklist items complete, with only the Devpost submission remaining. That's a very high plan-to-reality ratio for a 3–4 hour first build with no prior web development experience.

**What to try next time:** A few things drifted — the narrative quality issue (OCBC merchant formatting causing "Other" to dominate categories) was deferred to `/iterate`, and the login flow gap appeared at the end. These aren't spec failures; they're what happens when plan meets reality. The growth area is building in a deliberate "does the full flow feel right?" moment mid-build — not just do the individual pieces pass, but does the end-to-end experience hold together. The instinct to catch issues was clearly there (6+ product issues spotted during the breakdown build alone) — making it more structured would catch the higher-level gaps earlier.

## How You Worked

**What went well:** The process notes on this are unusually strong for a first-timer. The pivot from live bank API to statement upload was self-initiated. Investment advice was flagged as a legal issue before being asked. XP/levels tied to money were rejected on values grounds — "don't signal that more money = higher status." "Watchdog" was correctly identified as a misnomer for retrospective analysis. Six-plus issues were caught independently during the breakdown build. This project distinctly reflects a personal vision, not just what an AI generated — and the process notes make that visible.

**What to try next time:** The one place where agency was lower was in debugging loops — deferring to the agent when errors appeared is understandable for a first build. But as the quiz reflection surfaced: there's now enough experience to ask targeted technical questions ("the upload succeeds but the transactions table is empty — the extraction must be failing before it inserts"). Owning the diagnostic process, not just the product decisions, is the next level.

## Your Goals

You came in wanting to understand the end-to-end product shipping lifecycle, get hands dirty in a real but safe environment, and walk away with something to point to for PM roles.

Here's where that came through: the process notes show product-system thinking from day one — not just "what feature should I add" but "what are the legal constraints," "how does data flow," "what happens to a user who uploads and then leaves." The app is real, deployed, and structured in a way that shows the reasoning behind every major decision. That's the portfolio piece.

Bring the reflection document into PM interviews: "Here's a product I scoped, specced, and shipped in 4 hours. Here's what I cut and why. Here's what I'd do differently." Most PM candidates can't show that.

## Reflection

*On whether the goals were met:* The process and the planning helped scope the product into something that made sense for both users and builders — and having that context drove better outputs from the AI at every stage.

*On what surprised you most:* "How crazy that this became a reality — not just an idea in my head but something that is functional. Although I have other visions for it to be something greater than what it is today."

That's the right ending. Ideas stay ideas until they're real, and most people never close that gap. FinClarity is real. And knowing what v2 looks like isn't a gap — it's a roadmap.
